title: What are the essential JVM flags — `-Xms` (initial heap), `-Xmx` (max heap), `-XX:+UseG1GC` (choose GC), `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` (target pause), `-XX:MetaspaceSize` / `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` (class metadata limit)?
shortTitle: What are the essential JVM flags?

s1_definition.profdef: JVM flags configure the runtime at launch. `-Xms` sets the initial heap size and `-Xmx` sets the maximum heap size; setting them equal avoids runtime resizing. `-XX:+UseG1GC` selects the garbage collector. `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` sets G1's soft pause-time target. `-XX:MetaspaceSize` sets the threshold at which the first Metaspace garbage collection is triggered, and `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` caps how large Metaspace can grow. Together these control memory sizing, collection behavior, and class-metadata limits.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of launching the National Bank of India application like opening a branch and deciding its setup up front. `-Xms` is how much vault space you reserve on day one, and `-Xmx` is the most vault space you will ever allow. Choosing `-XX:+UseG1GC` is like hiring a particular cleaning crew, and `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` tells that crew never to lock the branch for more than a set number of minutes. The Metaspace flags decide how much office space the rulebooks describing accounts and transactions may occupy. Setting these wisely means the branch runs smoothly instead of constantly renovating or running out of room.
s1_definition.oneliner: `-Xms`/`-Xmx` size the heap, `-XX:+UseG1GC` picks the collector, `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` targets pause time, and the Metaspace flags bound class metadata.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** JVM flags configure the runtime at launch. `-Xms` sets the initial heap size and `-Xmx` sets the maximum heap size; setting them equal avoids runtime resizing. `-XX:+UseG1GC` selects the garbage collector. `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` sets G1's soft pause-time target. `-XX:MetaspaceSize` sets the threshold at which the first Metaspace garbage collection is triggered, and `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` caps how large Metaspace can grow. Together these control memory sizing, collection behavior, and class-metadata limits.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of launching the National Bank of India application like opening a branch and deciding its setup up front. `-Xms` is how much vault space you reserve on day one, and `-Xmx` is the most vault space you will ever allow. Choosing `-XX:+UseG1GC` is like hiring a particular cleaning crew, and `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` tells that crew never to lock the branch for more than a set number of minutes. The Metaspace flags decide how much office space the rulebooks describing accounts and transactions may occupy. Setting these wisely means the branch runs smoothly instead of constantly renovating or running out of room.

**One line to remember:** `-Xms`/`-Xmx` size the heap, `-XX:+UseG1GC` picks the collector, `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` targets pause time, and the Metaspace flags bound class metadata.

sections.s2_technical:
`-Xms` sets the heap size the JVM starts with, and `-Xmx` sets the absolute maximum it may grow to. If the application needs more than the current heap and it is below `-Xmx`, the JVM grows the heap, which involves work and can cause GC activity. In production I almost always set `-Xms` equal to `-Xmx`, for example `-Xms4g -Xmx4g`, so the heap is allocated once at startup and never resized, giving predictable behavior and avoiding resize pauses. Sizing `-Xmx` too small causes frequent GC and OutOfMemoryError; too large wastes memory and can lengthen pauses.

`-XX:+UseG1GC` explicitly selects the G1 collector. There are matching flags for other collectors: `-XX:+UseParallelGC`, `-XX:+UseZGC`, `-XX:+UseSerialGC`, and `-XX:+UseShenandoahGC`. Selecting the collector explicitly is good practice even when it is the default, because it documents intent and protects you if the default changes across JVM versions.

`-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` gives G1 a soft target for the maximum stop-the-world pause, defaulting to 200ms. G1 uses it to decide how much to collect per pause: a smaller value makes G1 collect fewer regions each time so pauses are shorter, but it collects more often, which can reduce throughput. It is a goal, not a guarantee.

`-XX:MetaspaceSize` sets the initial high-water mark at which the first Metaspace GC runs; after that the JVM adjusts the threshold. `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` caps Metaspace so a class-loading leak cannot consume unlimited native memory and take down the host. Without a cap, a leak (for example repeatedly loading classes) grows Metaspace until the machine runs out of native memory. A senior nuance: two more flags belong in every production setup even though they are not sizing flags — `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` with `-XX:HeapDumpPath` so you can diagnose an OOM after the fact, and `-Xlog:gc` so GC behavior is observable. Flags should be chosen from measurement and load testing, not copied blindly.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's transfer service was resizing its heap repeatedly under load, causing jitter in response times. This is exactly why we set `-Xms` equal to `-Xmx` — the heap is sized once and never renegotiated during trading hours.

Problem 2 — The service needs predictable pauses so customer transfers never appear to hang. This is exactly why we select G1 with `-XX:+UseG1GC` and give it a pause target with `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis`.

Problem 3 — A library that dynamically generated proxy classes slowly leaked class metadata, threatening to exhaust native memory. This is exactly why we cap `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` so the leak fails fast and visibly instead of crashing the whole host.

Our mini-project builds a `FlagInspectorDemo` that reads and logs the effective values of all these flags at runtime via `HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean` and `Runtime`, so the reader can launch it with different flag combinations and confirm exactly what the JVM is running with. A `JvmTuning` helper prints heap, GC, and Metaspace settings.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
jvm-flags-demo/
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/
            ├── FlagInspectorDemo.java     (main runnable demo)
            └── JvmTuning.java             (reads & prints effective flags)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/jvm/*.java

# Production-style launch with all essential flags set explicitly
java -Xms2g -Xmx2g \
     -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 \
     -XX:MetaspaceSize=128m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m \
     -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/log/bank/heap.hprof \
     -Xlog:gc:/var/log/bank/gc.log:time,uptime \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.FlagInspectorDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the launch command above, which fixes heap at 2GB, selects G1 with a 100ms pause target, bounds Metaspace between 128MB and 256MB, and enables heap dump on OOM.

Step 1 — The JVM starts and allocates a 2GB heap immediately because `-Xms` equals `-Xmx`. There will be no heap resizing during the run.

Step 2 — The JVM registers G1 as the active collector and records the 100ms pause target, which G1 will use to size each collection.

Step 3 — Metaspace begins with its first-collection threshold at 128MB and may grow no larger than 256MB. If class loading ever pushes it past 256MB, the JVM throws OutOfMemoryError in Metaspace rather than consuming unbounded native memory.

Step 4 — The safety flags arm a heap dump: if any OutOfMemoryError occurs, the JVM writes a .hprof file to the given path for later analysis in Eclipse MAT.

Step 5 — The demo's JvmTuning reads each effective value through HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean and Runtime and logs it, so an operator can confirm the container actually launched with the intended tuning.

Step 6 — The confirmation line logs that the service started with verified tuning, which in a real pipeline becomes a startup health check.

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Flag Inspection Design ═══

  ┌─ SOLID Applied ──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: JvmTuning only reads/reports configuration        │
  │  I: separate methods per concern (heap/GC/Metaspace)  │
  │  D: depends on HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean + Runtime       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────┐ reads ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │        JvmTuning         │──────▶│ HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean    │
  │ + printHeapSettings()    │       │ getVMOption(name)          │
  │ + printGcSettings()      │       │ Runtime.totalMemory()/max  │
  │ + printMetaspaceSettings()│      │ MemoryMXBean nonHeap       │
  │ + printSafetyFlags()     │       └──────────────────────────┘
  │ - opt(name): String      │
  └──────────────────────────┘

  Contract for opt(name):
    Pre:  name is a valid VM option
    Post: returns current value, or "n/a" if unavailable
    Never throws to caller (defensive)

  Call Chain:
  1. printHeapSettings()        [Runtime total/max → -Xms/-Xmx]
  2. printGcSettings()          [UseG1GC, MaxGCPauseMillis]
  3. printMetaspaceSettings()   [MetaspaceSize, MaxMetaspaceSize, used]
  4. printSafetyFlags()         [HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError, path]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The essential JVM flags fall into three groups: sizing the heap, choosing and tuning the garbage collector, and bounding class metadata. For the heap, `-Xms` sets the initial size and `-Xmx` sets the maximum, and in production I almost always set them equal, like `-Xms4g -Xmx4g`, so the heap is allocated once at startup and never resized during traffic, which removes a whole class of latency jitter. For the collector, `-XX:+UseG1GC` explicitly selects G1, and I set it explicitly even when it is the default so my intent is documented and safe across JVM versions. `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` gives G1 a soft target for the longest pause, and I remember it is a goal, not a guarantee, and that setting it too low just makes G1 collect more often and hurt throughput. For class metadata, `-XX:MetaspaceSize` sets the threshold for the first Metaspace collection and `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` caps it so a class-loading leak cannot eat unlimited native memory and crash the host.

The two flags I consider non-negotiable in production even though they are not sizing flags are `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` with a `-XX:HeapDumpPath`, so that when an OutOfMemoryError ever happens I automatically get a heap dump to analyze instead of losing the evidence, and `-Xlog:gc` so that GC behavior is observable from day one. And I always stress that flags should come from measurement and load testing, never from copying a config off the internet.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, I tuned our transfer service exactly this way. We had been seeing response-time jitter that turned out to be the heap resizing under load, so I pinned `-Xms` equal to `-Xmx`. We selected G1 with a modest pause target so transfers never appeared to hang. And after a proxy-generating library slowly leaked class metadata, I capped `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` so the leak would fail fast and visibly with a clear OutOfMemoryError in Metaspace, triggering an alert, rather than silently consuming native memory until the whole host fell over. Every one of those flags maps to a real production incident I have had to reason about.
